1.pericope_label: The burden of Damascus. Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it shall be a ruinous heap... And in that day it shall come to pass, that the glory of Jacob shall be made thin... Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the oracle in its history, recalling that Syria had been confederate with Ephraim against Judah under Ahaz and that the prophet had then foretold its overthrow by Assyria, a prediction already partly fulfilled, so that writing early in Hezekiah's reign he looks to a further fulfilment; the city of ancient days should lose its glory and be struck out, as it were, from the list of the great cities of the world. On the thinning of Jacob he notes the word is the one rendered impoverished elsewhere and that Jacob stands, as commonly in the prophets, for the northern kingdom, so that the figure is emaciation; on the reaper he admires the prophet's habit of localising his imagery, the valley named lying south-west of Jerusalem toward Bethlehem, famous for its fertility and often raided for its crops, so that the prophet had watched a reaper and seen in it a parable of the invader; and on the gleaning he finds the idea of the remnant held even for the northern kingdom, the vineyard supplying the first similitude and the olive-yard the second. Delitzsch explains why Israel is drawn into an oracle on Damascus: the curse falls on the northern kingdom too, because it had allied itself with heathen Damascus against its own brother tribe and against the Davidic government, and by that unnatural alliance with a stranger had become a stranger itself.

Gill takes the burden for a heavy and grievous prophecy of destruction, keeps Aroer as a real city by the Arnon, given by Moses to Reuben and Gad and since taken by the Syrians, and reports that a father of the church saw it still standing on a mountain top in his own day. He takes the fortress for Samaria, or for all their strongholds with the singular put for the plural, and cites the paraphrase that the government shall cease from Ephraim, so that they should have no more a king, nor have they to this day; he has the reaper gather the standing corn into one hand and cut it with the other, Israel being a field of corn for number, beauty and glory; and on the gleaning he holds for a few of the ten tribes escaping, reporting without adopting the rabbis who refer the few instead to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to Hezekiah's company, or to the survivors of the Assyrian army. Calvin gives the pastoral reason for recording such calamities at all, that the Jews, unable to contend with the Syrian king and stripped of other aid, might doubt whether God had abandoned them; makes Aroer the name of a country rather than the town mentioned elsewhere, drawing a picture of a land given over to pasture where only huts and shepherds' tents remain; says the harvest metaphor was chosen because a people trusting its numbers dreads nothing, as no reaper is daunted by the quantity of the corn; and marks the change of sense at the gleaning, where the prophet abates the severity he had just pronounced, since grapes are never gleaned so closely that none stay hidden under the leaves.

Clarke opens with a structural analysis of the whole chapter, observing that by its title the prophecy should relate only to Damascus but treats more largely of Samaria and the Israelites, and that its last three verses are a distinct piece worked up with great elegance on the sudden overthrow of Sennacherib. On Aroer he protests that the city on the Arnon has nothing to do with Damascus, that a second Aroer on Gad's northern border is little better, and that the cities of Aroer makes no sense if Aroer is itself a city; the Greek read the consonants as for ever, the old paraphrase as a verb meaning they shall be wasted, and the Syriac differently again, so that the reading is doubtful and he follows the Greek as plainest. He prefers a conjecture reading pride for remnant, since the sentence seems to require something answering to the glory of Israel, notes eight manuscripts and ten editions read in the glory, and reports a manuscript variant in the harvest verse. Wesley assigns the fulfilment to Tiglath-pileser while noting the city was afterwards rebuilt, explains that the Reubenites and Gadites who held the Aroer country were carried off by the same king and are mentioned because confederate with Syria, makes the survivors a headless body, a people without a king, and turns the comparison into a levelling, since Syria shall have as much glory as Israel, which is to say that neither shall have any.

Henry reads the title through the old paraphrase, the burden of the cup of the curse to drink to Damascus in, the ten tribes being in alliance and so bound to pledge Damascus in that cup of trembling; he expects the houses burnt, the walls and gates demolished and the inhabitants carried away, so that the head city is reduced not only to a village but to a ruinous heap, and remarks what desolating work sin makes with cities. On the gleaning he finds mercy reserved in a parenthesis in the midst of judgment: though the Assyrians took all the care they could that none should slip their net, the meek of the earth were hidden in the day of the Lord's anger and had their lives given them for a prey, made comfortable by their retirement into the land of Judah, where they had the liberty of God's courts.

positions.view: Probably not a place at all; the reading is doubtful and the Greek's for ever makes the plainest sense.
A real city by the Arnon, given to Reuben and Gad and later held by the Syrians.
The name of a country, not the town mentioned elsewhere, now given over to pasture.
A district of Syria named from a great city, whose towns the Reubenites and Gadites held until the captivity.

debates.question: How should the third verse, on the fortress and the remnant of Syria, be read?

positions.view: The fortress is Samaria, or all their strongholds; the paraphrase has the government cease from Ephraim, so they have no king to this day.
Read pride for remnant, which answers to the glory of Israel as the sentence seems to require.
A headless body without a king: Syria shall have as much glory as Israel, which is to say none.

debates.question: Who is left by the gleaning?

positions.view: A few of the ten tribes, though rabbis refer the survivors to Jerusalem, to Hezekiah's company, or to the remains of the Assyrian army.
The meek hidden in the day of the Lord's anger, who retired into Judah and had the liberty of God's courts.
The remnant, an idea the prophet holds even for the northern kingdom, figured first by the vineyard and then by the olive-yard.

outliers.note: Alone treats the chapter structurally, detaching the last three verses as a separate composition on Sennacherib before expounding a word of the oracle.
Grounds Israel's inclusion in the curse on a theology of the alliance: by joining a stranger against its own brother tribe, Israel had itself become a stranger.

themes: The burden of Damascus. Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it shall be a ruinous heap.
The cities of Aroer are forsaken: they shall be for flocks, which shall lie down, and none shall make them afraid.
The fortress also shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria: they shall be as the glory of the children of Israel, saith the Lord of hosts.
And in that day it shall come to pass, that the glory of Jacob shall be made thin, and the fatness of his flesh shall wax lean.
And it shall be as when the harvestman gathereth the corn, and reapeth the ears with his arm; and it shall be as he that gathereth ears in the valley of Rephaim.

Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outmost fruitful branches thereof, saith the Lord God of Israel.

7.pericope_label: At that day shall a man look to his Maker, and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel... Because thou hast forgotten the God of thy salvation... therefore shalt thou plant pleasant plants, and shalt set it with strange slips

schools.summary: Ellicott hears warning in the promise, since the return to the true faith of Israel is to be brought about by a bitter experience of the results of idolatry; identifies the objects abandoned as the conical tree-like pillars that symbolised a Canaanite goddess, the giver of good fortune, and the sun-images beside them; renders the strong cities a forsaken tract of forest and hill-top, the usual sites of fortresses, and grants that the Greek either followed a different reading or gives a curious paraphrase about the Amorites and Hivites. He finds the retribution exact, the rock of their strength contrasted with the rock-fortresses in which the people trusted, so that having forsaken the One they should lose the others; would render thou didst plant rather than thou shalt plant, notes that the word for pleasant occurs here only as a common noun and elsewhere as a personal name, most familiarly that of a Syrian, and infers that the prophet chose the peculiar term to mark the planting as Syrian, comparing the alliance in the rapidity of its growth to the gardens grown for a dying god; and holds that the harvest heaps end not in the wonted joy of harvest but in grief and incurable pain, with no sufficient evidence for the reading in the margin. Delitzsch prints the planting and the woe against the nations as one continuous movement.

Gill takes the man who looks to his Maker for the remnant according to the election of grace, and directs the looking to Christ, the Maker of all things, for righteousness, strength, pardon and salvation; reports the rabbi whom Clarke follows, who separated the clauses about the altars because otherwise all altars, even God's own, were the works of men and yet right to look to, and adds the application that a good man will not look to his own good works as altars to atone for sin. He has the strong cities forsaken of their inhabitants like a bough stripped of its leaves and a dead uppermost branch, lists the salvations forgotten in Egypt, at the Red Sea and since, and says of the planting that it is not in man's power to make anything grow, only that all means and methods should be used and no cost or pains spared. Calvin calls the turn to God the fruit of the chastisement and the second consolation with which the godly should fortify themselves, adding that when men betake themselves to God the world that was disordered is restored to its proper order; draws from the contrast that the looking of the previous verse means hope and confidence, since no one obtains a clear view of God except by driving far off every superstition, and that it is vain to think of uniting God and idols. He calls the view that the two obscure words are names of towns a forced interpretation, taking them rather for unpleasant places, so that walls and ditches would defend no better than thickets and bushes; states the cause without hedging, that the evils come because they wickedly despised God, an inexcusable ingratitude which prostituted their hopes to heathen nations and idols; and finds the verse on the growing ambiguous, rejecting the rendering that speaks of removing a branch on the day of affliction and taking the disputed noun in its plain sense of produce.

Clarke says the construction of the phrase about the altars is not obvious and that all the ancient versions and most of the modern have mistaken it: the word for work governs the word for altars rather than standing beside it, so that the sense is the altars of the work of their hands, that is, of the idols, an explanation he takes from a rabbi and a later scholar. On the strong cities he says no one has ever been able to make any tolerable sense of the two Hebrew words, that the Greek happily preserves what seems to be the true reading, the Amorites and the Hivites, and that many commentators who would never admit the Greek reading nonetheless expound the verse of that very event. He reads the pleasant plants and the shoots from a foreign soil allegorically, for strange and idolatrous worship with the vicious practices connected with it, and for reliance on human aid and alliances with the neighbouring nations, especially Egypt. Wesley keeps the plants literal, excellent flowers and fruit-trees fetched from far countries and therefore highly esteemed, says the few who are left shall trust and worship God and God only, notes that the pruner neglects the uppermost branch as useless, and observes that the Canaanites forsook their cities for fear of Israel, a fit example to awaken the Israelites since God had inflicted the same judgment for the same sins.

Henry presses the irony of the fortified cities: the strong cities which should have protected the country shall not be able to protect themselves, but will look like a forsaken bough and an uppermost branch of an old tree gone to decay, bare and dry and dead, once the inhabitants have deserted them and the enemy has pillaged and defaced them.

debates.question: How is the phrase about the altars and the work of his hands to be construed?

positions.view: The word for work governs the word for altars: the altars of the work of their hands, that is, of the idols.
The clauses are distinct, since otherwise God's own altars, being works of men, would fall under the same condemnation.
The objects named are the Asherah pillars of a Canaanite goddess and the sun-images.
Men's own inventions, and the groves devised as fit places for the worship of their gods.

debates.question: What do the two obscure words in the ninth verse mean?

positions.view: No tolerable sense has ever been made of them; the Greek preserves the true reading, the Amorites and the Hivites.
A forsaken tract of forest and hill-top, the usual sites of fortresses, left uninhabited and in ruins.
Not names of towns, which is forced, but disagreeable places: walls and ditches will defend no better than thickets.
The cities the Canaanites forsook for fear of Israel, cited as a warning example.
A bough stripped of its leaves and a dead uppermost branch, the cities emptied of inhabitants.

debates.question: What are the pleasant plants and the strange slips?

positions.view: A Syrian planting: the peculiar word marks it foreign, and the alliance grew as fast as the gardens grown for a dying god.
Allegorical for idolatrous worship and for reliance on alliances with neighbouring nations, especially Egypt.
Literal: excellent flowers and fruit-trees fetched from far countries and therefore highly esteemed.

outliers.note: Turns the abandoned altars into an application against trusting one's own good works as altars to atone for sin.
Comments on none of the disputed words, printing the planting and the woe against the nations as a single continuous movement.

themes: At that day shall a man look to his Maker, and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel.
And he shall not look to the altars, the work of his hands, neither shall respect that which his fingers have made, either the groves, or the images.
In that day shall his strong cities be as a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch, which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation.
Because thou hast forgotten the God of thy salvation, and hast not been mindful of the rock of thy strength, therefore shalt thou plant pleasant plants, and shalt set it with strange slips:
In the day shalt thou make thy plant to grow, and in the morning shalt thou make thy seed to flourish: but the harvest shall be a heap in the day of grief and of desperate sorrow.

12.pericope_label: Woe to the multitude of many people, which make a noise like the noise of the seas... And behold at eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us

schools.summary: Ellicott agrees with Clarke that the three verses stand as an isolated fragment, suggesting they were placed here because they begin like the opening of the next chapter, and that they may have been connected with the progress of Sennacherib's army; he also proposes that the parallel these verses present to the harvest of grief just before may have led to the insertion of the oracle in this place. He notes the rushing of mighty waters as an image for the march of an army has its parallel in an earlier chapter of the same prophet; would drop the supplied divine name, since inserting it weakens the force of the sublime indefiniteness of the Hebrew; identifies the rolling thing with the wheel of a psalm and takes it, like the chaff of the mountains, for the whirling dust-clouds driven from an elevated threshing-floor, denying any sufficient authority for the thistle-down of the margin; and says the words of the last verse, general as they are, received a special fulfilment in the destruction of the Assyrian army. Delitzsch prints the two closing verses without a word of comment.

Gill rules out two readings of the opening, that the prophet bemoans the Jews with Hezekiah and that the multitude means Syria and Israel combined against Judah, and settles on the Assyrian army under Sennacherib, made up of people of many nations and very numerous; he says a new subject is here begun, though a short one, and has the nations run over the whole land with great force and noise until they came to Jerusalem, where they stopped. On the trouble at eveningtide he reports the reading that places the terror in the Assyrian camp when the angel destroyed it, taking evening for night, and a rabbi who ascribes it to a sort of spirits or demons, but holds it best taken in the commoner sense, of the trouble Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem were in on the night before their deliverance, the country round about laid waste and the enemy blaspheming and triumphing. Calvin weighs the interjection: some render it as execration, and it is sometimes used in calling to a person, but he thinks it betokens sorrow, since the prophet groans over the calamity he foresees, whether out of brotherly affection or to press the threat on a sluggish and indolent people; the prophets, he adds, regarded God's vengeance with greater horror than other men and never laid aside human feelings so as not to pity those who perished. He insists the consolation is not for the Jews only, as is commonly supposed, since the discourse has been addressed to the ten tribes, among whom some still feared God and would have despaired without a promise; and he reads the last verse as a storm raised at sea and soon allayed, leaving no trace, stating two things, that the attack of the enemy will be sudden and that their ravages will not be of long duration.

Clarke says the three last verses seem to have no relation to the prophecy they are joined to, nor any connection with what follows, a beautiful piece standing singly and by itself, and he cannot say whether it stands in its right place; it is a noble description of the formidable invasion and the sudden overthrow of Sennacherib, in the strongest terms and the most expressive images, exactly suitable to the event. He then weighs the words: five of them, three ending one verse and two beginning the next, are omitted in eight manuscripts and the Syriac, so that the repetition is not made; and in the last verse he prefers a particle attested by many manuscripts, two editions and five versions, which restores the sentence to its true poetical form, at the season of evening behold terror, before the morning and behold he is no more. He adds that manuscripts and the Syriac read the singular in both nouns, him that spoileth us and him that robbeth us, which answers better to Sennacherib. Wesley calls it a new prophecy added for the comfort of God's people, takes the many as combined together against Judah, and reads the sea image of an invasion entering the land as the sea does by a breach.

Henry reads the passage as the doom of those that spoil and rob the people of God: if the Assyrians take God's people captive and lay their country waste, let them know that ruin will be their lot and portion. They relied upon their numbers, an army made up out of divers nations, by which weight they hoped to carry the cause; they were very noisy, like the roaring of the seas, talking big and threatening to frighten God's people from resisting them and their allies from sending aid, so that Sennacherib and his officer, in speeches and letters, made a mighty noise to strike terror into Hezekiah and his people.

debates.question: Do the last three verses belong where they stand?

positions.view: They have no relation to what precedes or follows; whether they stand in their right place he cannot say.
An isolated fragment, placed here because it opens like the next chapter, or from its parallel with the verse before.
A new subject is begun, though a short one.
A new prophecy, added for the comfort of God's people.

debates.question: What does the opening interjection express?

positions.view: Sorrow rather than execration: the prophet groans over the calamity he foresees, out of brotherly affection.
The doom pronounced on those who spoil and rob the people of God.

debates.question: What is the trouble at eveningtide?

positions.view: Hezekiah and Jerusalem on the night before their deliverance, though others place it in the Assyrian camp and a rabbi ascribes it to demons.
General words which received a special fulfilment in the destruction of the Assyrian army.
A sudden storm soon allayed: the attack is sudden and the ravages will not last.

outliers.note: Rebuilds the last verse from the manuscripts, restoring a particle to recover its poetic parallelism and preferring singular nouns that fit Sennacherib alone.
Prints the closing verses as a bare quotation, with no comment of any kind.

themes: Woe to the multitude of many people, which make a noise like the noise of the seas; and to the rushing of nations, that make a rushing like the rushing of mighty waters!

The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but God shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind.
And behold at eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us.
